context: Each move climbs 1 or 2 stairs, but two moves in a row cannot both climb 1. Whether we can climb 1 stair now depends on the previous move. We therefore use a two-dimensional state dp[i, j] to count the ways to reach stair i with a final move of j stairs, where j is 1 or 2.
description: The top stair shows two target states, dp[i, 1] in teal and dp[i, 2] in blue. Stair i-1 shows dp[i-1, 2] in teal and dp[i-1, 1] in gray. Stair i-2 shows dp[i-2, 1] and dp[i-2, 2] in blue. A solid teal arc climbs 1 stair from dp[i-1, 2] to dp[i, 1]. A gray dotted line from dp[i-1, 1] to dp[i, 1] is labeled “Two consecutive moves cannot both climb 1 stair, so omit this term.” Solid blue arcs from dp[i-2, 1] and dp[i-2, 2] each climb 2 stairs to dp[i, 2].

If the last move climbed 1 stair, it started on stair i-1, which must have been reached by climbing 2 stairs. Thus dp[i, 1] = dp[i-1, 2]. If the last move climbed 2 stairs, it started on stair i-2, which could have been reached by climbing either 1 or 2 stairs. Thus dp[i, 2] = dp[i-2, 1] + dp[i-2, 2].
The diagram shows symbolic transitions without initial values. The table below adds the initial states for stairs 1 and 2 used in the code that follows. The recurrence starts at stair 3.

frames.explanation: The only route to stair 1 is 0→1, so dp[1,1]=1 and dp[1,2]=0. For stair 2, the route 0→1→2 takes two consecutive one-stair moves and cannot count. Only 0→2 is valid, so dp[2,1]=0 and dp[2,2]=1.
frames.title: Extending the dynamic programming state with the length of the last move

result: Once the state includes the length of the last move, the available moves depend only on the current state. This restores the no-aftereffect property. The total number of ways to reach stair n is dp[n,1] + dp[n,2].
summary: A two-dimensional state dp[i, j] records whether the last move climbed 1 or 2 stairs, so the transition can rule out consecutive one-stair moves.
